nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet and teacher writing in English
literary_identity: American poet of the Michigan greenhouses and the Pacific Northwest, whose rhythmic, hypnotic verse moved from the greenhouse poems to the love poems and the mystical sequences of his last books
biography: Theodore Huebner Roethke was born in Saginaw, Michigan, on 25 May 1908, the son of a German immigrant who owned greenhouses, and grew up among them; his father and uncle both died in 1923, when he was fourteen. He took his BA at the University of Michigan in 1929 and his MA in 1936, studied briefly at Harvard and the University of Michigan Law School, and taught at Lafayette College, Pennsylvania State University, Bennington College and, from 1947 until his death, at the University of Washington, where he became poet in residence in 1962. Open House (1941), The Lost Son and Other Poems (1948), Praise to the End! (1951), The Waking (1953, Pulitzer Prize), Words for the Wind (1958, National Book Award) and I Am! Says the Lamb (1961) appeared in his lifetime, and The Far Field (1964, National Book Award) posthumously. He suffered from manic depression throughout his life, was a celebrated and demanding teacher, and died on Bainbridge Island, Washington, on 1 August 1963.
literary_profile: Poetry: Open House (1941), The Lost Son and Other Poems (1948), Praise to the End! (1951), The Waking: Poems 1933-1953 (1953), Words for the Wind (1958), I Am! Says the Lamb (1961) and The Far Field (1964). Prose: On the Poet and His Craft (1965, selected prose) and Straw for the Fire (1972, notebooks).
stylistic_characteristics: Strongly rhythmic, often hypnotic free verse with heavy stresses and internal rhyme; short lines and nursery-rhyme cadences set against long Whitmanian sequences; exact natural notation (roots, stems, greenhouse glass, animals); fixed forms - the villanelle, the ballad - used alongside the loose 'lost son' sequences.
intellectual_concerns: Growth, decay and the vegetable world of the greenhouse; the dead father and the childhood garden; love, the body and the erotic; the mystical and the primitive; madness, the unconscious and the journey inward; the American landscape of Michigan and the Northwest.
historical_significance: Roethke is the central American poet of the 'middle generation' between the modernists and the confessional poets, and his greenhouse poems and 'The Waking' are among the most anthologised American poems of the century; his fusion of the child's eye with a mystical ambition influenced Lowell, Plath and a long line of later poets.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Roethke, read directly; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selections - 'Cuttings' and 'Cuttings (later)' (The Lost Son, 1948), 'The Waking' and 'Elegy for Jane' (The Waking, 1953) and 'I Knew a Woman' (Words for the Wind, 1958); 'My Papa's Waltz' (1942) is before the period, and the other collections have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, short-story writer, painter and translator writing in English
literary_identity: American poet of exact observation and deliberate reticence, whose few, slowly written poems of travel, loss and childhood are among the most admired in twentieth-century American verse
biography: Elizabeth Bishop was born in Worcester, Massachusetts, on 8 February 1911; her father died when she was eight months old and her mother was institutionalised in 1916, and she was raised by her maternal grandparents in Great Village, Nova Scotia, and then by relatives in Massachusetts. She took her AB at Vassar College in 1934, travelled in Europe and North Africa, lived in Key West and, from 1951, in Brazil, where she lived with the architect Lota de Macedo Soares until 1967, and settled in Boston in the 1970s, teaching at Harvard. North and South (1946), Poems: North & South - A Cold Spring (1955, Pulitzer Prize), Questions of Travel (1965), Complete Poems (1969, National Book Award) and Geography III (1976, National Book Critics Circle Award) are the volumes of her lifetime, with The Complete Poems 1927-1979 (1983) and the prose of The Collected Prose (1984) afterwards; she was Consultant in Poetry to the Library of Congress in 1949-50 and received the Neustadt International Prize in 1976. She died in Boston on 6 October 1979.
literary_profile: Poetry: North and South (1946), Poems: North & South - A Cold Spring (1955), Questions of Travel (1965), The Complete Poems (1969), Geography III (1976) and The Complete Poems 1927-1979 (1983). Prose: The Collected Prose (1984) and the letters in One Art (1994). Translations: The Diary of Helena Morley (1957) and An Anthology of Twentieth-Century Brazilian Poetry (1972, with Emanuel Brasil).
stylistic_characteristics: Quiet, exactly observed free verse and strict forms - the villanelle, the sestina, the sonnet - used without display; a painter's eye for colour, edge and perspective; understatement, reticence and a refusal of confessional exposure; a plain syntax that carries sudden metaphysical turns.
intellectual_concerns: Travel and the ethics of the observer; childhood, orphanhood and the loss of the mother; the discipline of loss and the making of art from it; the particularity of places - Nova Scotia, Florida, Brazil, New England; maps, geography and the frames through which a life is seen; dreams and surreal detail.
historical_significance: Bishop is among the most admired American poets of the century and the model of a poet's poet: her reticence, her formal control and her exactness are the standards against which later American verse is often measured, and 'One Art', 'In the Waiting Room' and 'The Armadillo' are canonical texts in the study of the villanelle, of the late style and of postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Bishop, read directly, and from the sources cited for the individual poems; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selections - 'At the Fishhouses' (1947), 'Questions of Travel' (1956), 'The Armadillo' (1957), 'In the Waiting Room' (1971) and 'One Art' (New Yorker, 1976); 'The Fish' (1940) is before the period, and the prose has no record, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; playwright, poet, short-story writer and screenwriter writing in English
literary_identity: American playwright of the American South whose lyrical, violent dramas of desire and delusion - above all A Streetcar Named Desire and Cat on a Hot Tin Roof - made him the central playwright of postwar Broadway
biography: Thomas Lanier Williams III was born in Columbus, Mississippi, on 26 March 1911 and grew up in Mississippi and in St Louis, where his father managed a shoe warehouse; he studied at the University of Missouri, Washington University and the University of Iowa, where he took a BA in 1938. The Glass Menagerie opened in Chicago in 1944 and in New York in 1945; A Streetcar Named Desire followed on Broadway on 3 December 1947 and won the Pulitzer Prize in 1948, and Summer and Smoke (1948), The Rose Tattoo (1951), Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1955, Pulitzer Prize), Orpheus Descending (1957), Suddenly Last Summer (1958), Sweet Bird of Youth (1959), The Night of the Iguana (1961) and The Milk Train Doesn't Stop Here Anymore (1963) followed, with the later plays, the screenplays of Baby Doll (1956) and others, and the stories and memoirs. He died in a New York hotel on 25 February 1983.
literary_profile: Plays: The Glass Menagerie (1944), A Streetcar Named Desire (1947), Summer and Smoke (1948), The Rose Tattoo (1951), Camino Real (1953), Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1955), Orpheus Descending (1957), Suddenly Last Summer (1958), Sweet Bird of Youth (1959), The Night of the Iguana (1961), The Milk Train Doesn't Stop Here Anymore (1963) and Small Craft Warnings (1972). Screenplays: Baby Doll (1956), Suddenly, Last Summer (1959) and others. Prose: One Arm (1948, stories), Hard Candy (1954, stories), The Roman Spring of Mrs Stone (1950, novel) and Memoirs (1975).
stylistic_characteristics: A lyrical, rhetorical, image-rich dialogue that raises Southern speech into poetry; long monologues and confession scenes; expressionist staging - the transparent walls of Menagerie, the screeching streetcar and the polka of Streetcar; violent contrasts of tenderness and brutality; symbols carried by light, sound and costume.
intellectual_concerns: Desire, delusion and the refusal of reality; the dying Southern aristocracy and its illusions; the brutality of the sexual and the social world; homosexuality, guilt and self-punishment; memory, time and the fragility of art; loneliness, alcoholism and madness.
historical_significance: Williams is the major American dramatist of the postwar decades and, with Miller, the playwright through whom the American theatre of the 1940s and 1950s is studied; Streetcar's Blanche DuBois and Stanley Kowalski are among the great roles of the modern stage, the 1951 Kazan film with Marlon Brando fixed the play in popular memory, and the play's language and staging changed what American drama could do with desire and memory.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Williams and on A Streetcar Named Desire, read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, A Streetcar Named Desire (1947); the other plays, the films and the prose have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer and novelist writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer and novelist, the 'Chekhov of the suburbs', whose stories of Westchester County and the Upper East Side turned the disappointments of the American middle class into fable
biography: John William Cheever was born in Quincy, Massachusetts, on 27 May 1912 and grew up in Wollaston; his father's shoe business failed in the 1920s. He was expelled from Thayer Academy at seventeen - the episode became his first story, 'Expelled' (1930) - and began publishing in The New Yorker in the 1930s. The Wapshot Chronicle (1957, National Book Award), The Wapshot Scandal (1964, William Dean Howells Medal), Bullet Park (1969), Falconer (1977) and the novella Oh What a Paradise It Seems (1982) are the novels; the stories are gathered in The Enormous Radio (1953), The Housebreaker of Shady Hill (1958), Some People, Places, and Things That Will Not Appear in My Next Novel (1961), The Brigadier and the Golf Widow (1964) and The Stories of John Cheever (1978, Pulitzer Prize, National Book Critics Circle Award and National Book Award). He taught at the Iowa Writers' Workshop and at Sing Sing prison, was awarded the National Medal for Literature in 1982, and died at Ossining, New York, on 18 June 1982.
literary_profile: Novels: The Wapshot Chronicle (1957), The Wapshot Scandal (1964), Bullet Park (1969), Falconer (1977) and Oh What a Paradise It Seems (1982). Story collections: The Way Some People Live (1943), The Enormous Radio (1953), The Housebreaker of Shady Hill (1958), Some People, Places, and Things That Will Not Appear in My Next Novel (1961), The Brigadier and the Golf Widow (1964) and The Stories of John Cheever (1978). Journals: The Journals of John Cheever (1991) and the letters (1988).
stylistic_characteristics: A lucid, elegant, faintly ironic prose that keeps a straight face while the events turn fantastic; exact social notation of clothes, drinks, commuter trains and lawns; a habit of sudden mythic or apocalyptic imagery inside an ordinary scene; dialogue that exposes class and self-deception.
intellectual_concerns: Suburban America, its comforts and its terrors; the disparity between the social mask and the inner life; alcoholism, infidelity and the collapse of the family; nostalgia for an older New England community; the fantastic and the mythic intruding into the everyday; the sadness of the commuter's life.
historical_significance: Cheever is the defining short-story writer of the American suburbs and one of the great American story writers of the century; 'The Swimmer' is his most anthologised story and is regularly read as an American fable of decline, and The Stories of John Cheever, which won the Pulitzer Prize, established the short story as a serious American literary form in the postwar decades.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Cheever, read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'The Swimmer' (The New Yorker, 18 July 1964; collected in The Brigadier and the Golf Widow, 1964); the novels and the other stories have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, essayist and teacher writing in English
literary_identity: American poet of the Bahá'í faith and of African American history, whose formally exact poems on the Middle Passage, Frederick Douglass and his own childhood made him the first Black Consultant in Poetry to the Library of Congress
biography: Robert Hayden was born Asa Bundy Sheffey in Detroit on 4 August 1913 and was raised by a foster family, Sue Ellen and William Hayden, in the Paradise Valley neighbourhood. He studied at Detroit City College and at the University of Michigan, where he took an MA in 1942 under W. H. Auden and won a Hopwood Award, and taught at Fisk University from 1946 to 1969 and then at the University of Michigan until his death. Heart-Shape in the Dust (1940), Figure of Time (1955), A Ballad of Remembrance (1962), Selected Poems (1966), Words in the Mourning Time (1970), The Night-Blooming Cereus (1972), Angle of Ascent (1975) and American Journal (1978) are the collections; he was Consultant in Poetry to the Library of Congress from 1976 to 1978, the first African American to hold the post, and died in Ann Arbor on 25 February 1980.
literary_profile: Poetry: Heart-Shape in the Dust (1940), Figure of Time (1955), A Ballad of Remembrance (1962), Selected Poems (1966), Words in the Mourning Time (1970), The Night-Blooming Cereus (1972), Angle of Ascent (1975) and American Journal (1978), with Collected Poems (1985, ed. Frederick Glaysher). Prose: Collected Prose (1984).
stylistic_characteristics: Formal, metrically regular verse - the sonnet, the ballad, the quatrain - with strong rhymes and refrains; a historical and documentary method that assembles ship logs, testimonies and voices; a restrained, meditative tone; dense imagery drawn from slavery, the Bible and Bahá'í scripture.
intellectual_concerns: The Middle Passage and the history of slavery; African American heroism, above all Frederick Douglass and the Amistad rebels; the father and the childhood home in Detroit; the Bahá'í teaching of the unity of humanity and its rejection of racial separatism; the American past, its monuments and its violence.
historical_significance: Hayden is a central figure of twentieth-century African American poetry and the one who most firmly resisted the demand that Black poetry be only protest; 'Middle Passage' is the founding modern poem of the slave trade in American literature, and 'Those Winter Sundays' is among the most widely taught American poems of any period.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Hayden and on 'Middle Passage', read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selections 'Those Winter Sundays' and 'Summertime and the Living . . .' (A Ballad of Remembrance, 1962); 'Middle Passage' was first published in 1945 and is outside the period, though Norton prints the 1962 revision. The other collections have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.
